title: Butter Chicken, Biggie Smalls, and a Venice Beach Opening: Inside the 'Progressive Indian' Movement Rewriting America's Curry Script
excerpt: A new wave of Indian restaurants — from Badmaash in Los Angeles to Indibar in Phoenix — is blowing up the burgundy-carpet stereotype and betting that the diaspora's food deserves the same respect as French and Japanese fine dining.
body:
The newest Badmaash restaurant sits on Venice Beach's Abbot Kinney Boulevard, where the soundtrack is old-school hip-hop, a Pop Art Gandhi wears Ray-Ban Wayfarers, and the dessert menu includes ice cream sandwiches made with Parle-G biscuits. There is no burgundy carpet. There is no sitar music. There is no $6.99 all-you-can-eat lunch buffet.

"Your idea of an Indian restaurant is f***ing horrible," co-founder Nakul Mahendro told Restaurant Business earlier this year, summarising the mission statement that he, his brother Arjun, and their 72-year-old father Pawan — still slamming pans in the kitchen "like he's 25" — have been living since they opened the first Badmaash in downtown LA in 2013. "Don't put me in that box."

## Context and Background

The word *badmaash* means scoundrel or hooligan in Hindi — a term of endearment that the Mahendro family chose precisely because they intended to break every rule. When they launched the original downtown location, Arjun and Nakul printed the hashtag #fuckyourfavoriteIndianrestaurant on their menus. On the food side, they served Punjabi-spiced steak frites alongside butter chicken, and a lamb burger designed so that, as Nakul puts it, the "typically less adventurous" date at the table could say, "Look, honey, there's a burger on the menu."

The Venice Beach expansion, which opened in late May, marks their third location and most ambitious yet — a full bar with a cocktail program featuring bourbon-based drinks spiced with Madeira and housemade date jam. A fourth concept, Secret Indian Food Window by Badmaash, operates out of the Pacific Electric music venue in Chinatown, serving Indian tacos: butter chicken, short rib curry, and Indian beef chorizo.

## The Progressive Indian Wave

Badmaash is not alone. 2026 has been called "the year of redefining Indian food in America" by Restaurant Business, and the evidence is everywhere.

In Phoenix, Indibar by Masti Hospitality — led by chefs Nigel Lobo and Ajay Singh — is preparing to launch Lehr this fall, a restaurant-within-a-restaurant offering 10-course tasting menus designed to take 22 guests on a journey through India's regions. In Los Angeles, Rivaaz Hospitality, the group behind Rooh Progressive Indian in San Francisco and Fitoor in Palo Alto, has launched a national luxury catering division to bring its modern take on Indian food to weddings and corporate events.

From the United Kingdom, Dishoom — a 12-unit chain reportedly valued at nearly $400 million after a private-equity investment from L Catterton — is set to open in New York City later this year. JKS Restaurants brought its two-Michelin-starred Gymkhana concept to Las Vegas' Aria Resort and Casino in December, and followed with its Punjabi-focused Ambassadors Clubhouse in New York.

## Diaspora Impact

For NRIs who grew up watching their parents' cooking dismissed as "just curry," the progressive Indian movement carries emotional weight that goes beyond restaurant reviews.

Mahendro traces the lineage back to Floyd Cardoz's Tabla, which opened in 1998 as part of Danny Meyer's Union Square Hospitality Group and earned three stars from the New York Times — only to close in 2010. "That restaurant was 20 years before its time," Mahendro said.

But he is quick to note that the fight is far from won. "The Indian chef is not as respected as the Italian chef or the French chef," he said. "When I say 'three-star Michelin chef,' you still picture a French dude in chef whites." The US has yet to produce an Indian chef with the household name recognition of a Nobu Matsuhisa or a Michael Chow.

The Mahendro family's own story — Chef Pawan trained at Mumbai's Institute of Hotel Management, cooked at the Taj Mahal Intercontinental, ran restaurants from Toronto to New York, and came out of retirement because his sons convinced him their vision needed his palate — is a diaspora arc in miniature.

## What's Next

The progressive Indian movement's next frontier may be fast-casual. In Raleigh, the Chai Pani Restaurant Group just opened Botiwalla, its Indian street food concept, on June 2. In Cary, North Carolina, Desi Chowrastha debuted with biryani and curries. In Worcester, Massachusetts, Indian Bites took over a public market stall and is serving samosas and naan to the lunch crowd.

If the $400-million valuation of Dishoom is any guide, investors are betting that Indian food's breakout moment in America is not a question of if but when. For the Mahendro family, the answer is simpler. "Something good is happening," said Chef Sujan Sarkar, who is bringing his Michelin-starred Indienne from Chicago to New York. "You'll see it evolve and get better."

For now, at least, they are letting Biggie Smalls do the talking.
